claims.text: Rapidly quenched FeCoNiTi has an fcc matrix containing hexagonal C14 Laves-phase precipitates.
The FeCoNiTi alloy exhibits ferromagnetic transitions near 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
Coexistence of the C14 Laves phase significantly increases the coercivity of FeCoNiTi.
The Ti-rich sublattice of the C14 phase couples antiferromagnetically to Fe, Co, and Ni moments in the adjacent fcc matrix.
An interaction involving an antiferromagnetic constituent can reduce saturation magnetization while increasing coercivity.
The fcc/C14 interfaces act as strong magnetic domain-wall pinning centers.
Increasing the C14 phase fraction and Ti concentration increases interfacial area and modulates inter-sublattice exchange strength.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations are present in the fcc FeCoNiTi phase at elevated temperature.
Hybridization between Ti 3d states in the C14 phase and Fe/Co 3d states in the fcc phase mediates interfacial magnetic pinning.
Ti in the C14 phase carries a local magnetic moment.
Interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling reduces the effective magnetic moment per atom in the fcc phase.
Interfacial antiferromagnetic coupling creates a high energy barrier for domain-wall motion and thereby raises coercivity above 100 Oe.
The dual-phase alloy will have a coercivity of approximately 667 Oe at 400 K, whereas a single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi control will remain below 100 Oe.
The saturation magnetization will decrease in proportion to the C14 phase volume fraction.
Single-phase fcc FeCoNiTi has coercivity capped at 100 Oe because of insufficient orbital moments and a lack of pinning mechanisms.
The proposed mechanism requires a thermodynamically stable C14 phase with coherent or semi-coherent fcc/C14 interfaces.
Excessive Ti can promote amorphous phases or incoherent oxide inclusions that disrupt the proposed electronic coupling.
A first-principles fcc/C14 interface calculation should compare spin-resolved density of states at the Fermi level and calculate the Ti-Fe exchange coupling.
A reduction in majority-spin density of states or formation of a pseudogap at the Fermi level would indicate antiferromagnetic hybridization.

Comparing high-C14 and negligible-C14 FeCoNiTi samples using temperature-dependent magnetometry, XMCD, and magnetic-force microscopy can test phase-specific transitions, element-specific alignment, and interfacial pinning.
